title: File Handling
relevance: File I/O is a core Python skill for OAs and SDE interviews because persistence, modes, and safe resource cleanup show up in coding tasks and follow-ups.

phases.goal: Establish that open() yields a file object, modes control intent, and close() releases the file.

must_hit.point: The built-in open() function accesses files and returns a file object.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says open() returns a file object used for subsequent reads/writes.

must_hit.point: close() flushes in-memory buffers and releases the file back to the operating system.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions flushing buffers and releasing the OS resource on close().

must_hit.point: Mode 'r' is read (default) and errors if the file does not exist; 'w' truncates then writes; 'x' is exclusive creation that fails if the file exists; 'a' appends; 'b' is binary; 't' is text (default).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Can list the mode characters and their meanings without inventing extra modes.

probes: What does open() return, and what do the common mode characters mean?

hints.1: Think about how you get a handle to a file and what the second argument to open() controls.
hints.2: Map each mode character: read default, write-with-truncate, exclusive create, append, binary, text.
hints.3: open() returns a file object; close() flushes buffers and releases the file to the OS; 'r'/'w'/'x'/'a'/'b'/'t' match the mode table.

phases.goal: Show how read, readline, writelines, and the with context manager actually move data and close files.

must_hit.point: read() loads the entire file content into a single string; passing a count reads that many characters and later calls continue from where the previous left off.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes full-file read() and that a sized read advances the file position for subsequent calls.

must_hit.point: readline() returns the next line on each call; an empty string signals end when looping line by line.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains successive readline() calls and stopping when data == ''.

must_hit.point: writelines() writes a list of strings directly into a file.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says writelines() takes a list of strings and writes them without inventing extra APIs.

must_hit.point: A with open(...) as f block is a context manager that automatically and safely closes the file when the indented block finishes, including on error.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States that with closes the file automatically when the block ends, so manual close() is unnecessary.

probes: How do read(), readline(), and with open(...) as f differ in what they return and when the file is closed?

hints.1: Compare reading everything at once versus one line at a time, then how with changes cleanup.
hints.2: read() → one string (optional size continues later); readline() → next line until ''; with closes when the block exits.
hints.3: Full answer: read()/sized read with continuing position; readline() until ''; writelines() for a list; with auto-closes on normal exit or error.

phases.goal: Contrast write vs append, manual close vs with, and loading a whole file vs reading in chunks.

must_hit.point: 'w' erases existing contents before writing; 'a' adds new data without erasing existing content.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Clearly contrasts truncate-on-open write mode with append mode.

must_hit.point: Manual close() is error-prone because a crash before close() can leave the file open, causing resource leaks or corrupted data; with closes automatically.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Links crash-before-close risks to preferring the context manager.

must_hit.point: read() on a massive file tries to load the entire file into RAM and can crash the system; chunked reads keep only a manageable slice in memory.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Warns that full read() can exhaust memory on huge files and recommends looping with a fixed chunk size.

probes: When would you choose 'w' versus 'a', and why prefer with or chunked reads over manual close and a single read()?

hints.1: Ask what happens to existing file contents under each write-related mode, then what fails if close never runs.
hints.2: 'w' truncates; 'a' appends; with auto-closes; chunk loops avoid loading gigabyte-scale files wholesale.
hints.3: Prefer 'a' to keep old data, with for safe closure, and chunked read so only a small buffer stays in memory.

phases.goal: Apply chunked reading so only a fixed-size buffer stays in memory for large files.

must_hit.point: For large files, loop with read(chunk_size), continuing while the returned chunk has length greater than 0.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes a while loop that prints/processes each chunk and re-reads until an empty chunk.

must_hit.point: Using chunk_size of 100 means only 100 characters are kept in memory at any given time, regardless of file size.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States that a chunk size of 100 caps in-memory content at 100 characters per read.

probes: How would you read a multi-gigabyte text file without loading it all into RAM?

hints.1: Avoid a single unbounded read(); think about repeatedly reading a fixed amount.
hints.2: with open(...), set chunk_size, read that many characters, loop while the chunk is non-empty.
hints.3: with open('big.txt','r') as f: chunk = f.read(100); while len(chunk) > 0: process; chunk = f.read(100).

tradeoffs.strong_answer: 'w' truncates any existing file then writes; 'a' opens for writing at the end so new data is added without erasing prior content.

tradeoffs.topic: Manual close() vs with context manager
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Manual close() can be skipped if the program crashes first, risking leaks or corruption; with automatically and safely closes when the block ends, even on error.
read() loads the whole file into RAM and can crash on massive files; looping with a fixed chunk size keeps only that chunk in memory.

gotchas.trap: Attempting to read or write after close()
gotchas.correction: That raises ValueError: I/O operation on closed file.

gotchas.trap: Using 'w' when you meant to keep existing data
gotchas.correction: 'w' erases the entire existing contents before writing; use 'a' to append.

gotchas.trap: Calling read() on a gigabyte-scale file
gotchas.correction: It tries to load the entire file into RAM and can crash the system; read in chunks instead.

gotchas.trap: Relying on a late f.close() after possible failures
gotchas.correction: If the program crashes before close(), the file may stay open; use with so closure always happens when the block finishes.
